candidates.title: Culture Plate
candidates.pitch: A glowing petri dish under a blacklight holds a live Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion culture. The visitor inoculates it with a fingertip, then steers its chemistry by dragging a marker across a hand-labelled feed/kill map whose regions are named like pantry items (spots, worms, coral, bubbling, mitosis). A slow drift mode lets the culture ferment from one regime to the next, and a poster mode stamps the result with a museum-style specimen label and a shareable seed.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless: reaction-diffusion is the most photogenic bit of mathematics on the web, and an autumn-dark ultraviolet palette with a lab-specimen framing gives it a point of view that differs from the stock demos.

research.summary: Gray-Scott is a two-chemical model on a grid: chemical A is fed in at rate f, chemical B is removed at rate k, and B converts A. Per Karl Sims's tutorial, a 3x3 Laplacian with weights -1 centre, 0.2 edges, 0.05 corners (summing to zero) is enough, and typical values are DA=1.0, DB=0.5, f=0.055, k=0.062. The (f, k) plane is a known map of regimes: spots, stripes, waves, worms, solitons, solid regions. Exact coordinates differ between implementations (grid size, step, diffusion constants), so the page will calibrate its own map and label presets as this page's calibration. Prior art exists (Sims's RD Tool, a Google experiment, a Frankfurt applet), so the value lies in the point of view: the named map, drift mode, contamination brush, specimen-label poster and shareable seed. Model limits: a toy two-species chemistry on a flat grid, not real fermentation; Turing-type mechanisms are plausible for fish pigment stripes but evidence elsewhere (for example digits) is mostly simulation-based.

sources.title: Reaction-Diffusion Tutorial (Karl Sims)
sources.snippet: Tutorial describing chemical A fed at rate f and chemical B removed at rate k on a grid, with a 3x3 Laplacian kernel and suggested starting values for diffusion, feed and kill.
sources.note: Primary reference for the update rule and kernel weights

sources.title: Reaction Diffusion: The Gray-Scott Algorithm (Algosome)
sources.snippet: Independent write-up giving the same 3x3 kernel (centre -1, edges 0.2, corners 0.05) and explaining the multiply-and-sum step per neighbour.
sources.note: Second independent source agreeing on the Laplacian kernel

sources.title: Pearson classes (Robert Munafo, xmorphia)
sources.snippet: Describes the feed/kill map: moving along the kill axis at fixed feed shifts the culture between solid regions, stripes and spots; very low feed is too chaotic.
sources.note: Establishes that the (f,k) plane is a map of pattern regimes

sources.title: Pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems using the Gray-Scott model (Univ. Frankfurt student project)
sources.snippet: Student project listing example (F,k) pairs and their outcomes such as spots, loops, solitons, waves and worms.
sources.note: Independent confirmation that named regimes exist at specific f,k pairs; numbers vary by implementation

sources.title: RDTool example Reaction-Diffusion Explorer Tool (Karl Sims)
sources.snippet: Help page for an interactive Gray-Scott explorer with presets and drawing controls; needs WebGL 2 with a float colour-buffer extension.
sources.note: Prior art to differentiate from; shows the GPU route needs a CPU/worker fallback

sources.title: Gray-Scott Simulation (Google Experiments)
sources.snippet: A published interactive Gray-Scott experiment where feed and kill rates can be adjusted.
sources.note: Second independent piece of prior art

sources.title: Turing patterns in biology review (PMC3303118)
sources.snippet: Review stating reaction-diffusion simulations reproduce zebrafish stripes, digits, teeth and shells, while noting experimental tests are scarce and much support is resemblance.
sources.note: Supports a cautious 'plausible in nature' about-panel line

sources.title: Turing bifurcation and zebrafish stripes (Nature Communications)
sources.snippet: Paper arguing zebrafish pigment patterns arise from a Turing bifurcation driven by differential growth.
sources.note: Independent second source on zebrafish stripes

facts.claim: In the Gray-Scott model one chemical is fed in at rate f and the other removed at rate k; the common discrete Laplacian is a 3x3 kernel with centre -1, edges 0.2 and corners 0.05, which sums to zero (as of 2026-10-10).
The feed and kill rates decide which regime appears (spots, stripes, waves, worms, solitons, solid regions); exact coordinates differ between implementations, so presets are examples.
Interactive Gray-Scott explorers already exist, including a WebGL 2 tool with presets and a Google experiment with adjustable feed and kill rates.
Zebrafish stripe patterns are treated as Turing-type systems in the literature, though the molecular basis is still debated and much other evidence is simulation-based.

design.coreLoop: Seed a dish with a fingertip, pick a spot on the feed/kill map, watch the culture settle into a regime, then nudge, drift or contaminate it to see it transform. The map is the second-minute reward (each region behaves differently and has a name), drift mode and the contamination brush are the tenth-minute reward (staged mishaps make new hybrids), and the poster button gives a keepable specimen print with a seed in the URL hash.
sophisticationHooks: Hand-calibrated feed/kill map with named regimes and a draggable marker, plus a ferment-drift mode that slowly walks the marker along a path across regimes
Brush tools that act locally on chemistry: inoculate (add B), nutrient spill (add A), poison (raise kill), so mishaps become compositional tools
Specimen-poster export: ultraviolet palette, generated catalogue number and Latin-style name derived deterministically from f, k and seed, with the full state in the URL hash
Pure numerical core (init, step, state, reset) running fixed timesteps with seeded noise in a worker, a mass-conservation-style sanity clamp and no NaN reaching the canvas
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: Gray-Scott core on a 256x256 grid in a worker (about 8 steps per frame), canvas2d palette renderer with 3 colour ramps, feed/kill map canvas with about 12 named regions, brushes, drift mode, hash state (f, k, seed, palette, painted dots), PNG poster export, light/dark and reduced-motion handling, about/making-of panel. Cut: WebGL path, 3D view, audio, saving galleries.
risks: Preset f,k coordinates vary between implementations; the page labels regions as its own calibration and tests each by running the core headless before shipping.
Pearson's Greek-letter class labels were not confirmed in a source seen today, so the page uses its own names and does not cite Pearson's letters.
CPU simulation on low-end phones: cap grid at 256x256 and drop to 192 if frame time exceeds budget.
Prior art exists, so differentiation depends on the named map, drift mode, brushes and poster polish rather than on the simulation itself.
Biology line in the about panel must stay cautious (plausible, partly simulation-based) and the page must say it is a toy chemistry, not real fermentation.

candidates.title: Unreliable Plotter
candidates.pitch: A virtual pen plotter draws a generative poster line by line on screen: flow-field ribbons, L-system shrubs or spiral-packed circles, each in two or three pens. The twist is a mishap dial that lets the machine misbehave in physically motivated ways (a pen drying out and skipping, a blot on touchdown, paper creeping between pen swaps), narrated by a deadpan operator log. The visitor hunts for the dial setting where the imperfections make the poster better than the ideal version, then shares the seed or saves the layered SVG.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless: pen-plotter flow-field art is a recognised craft scene, and treating machine error as a creative parameter is a fresh angle on a familiar genre.

research.summary: A flow field is a grid of direction vectors, usually angles taken from Perlin noise, along which particles are traced to produce smooth curves; the technique is widely used and suits plotters because each curve is one continuous pen stroke. Plotter workflows separate artwork into SVG layers that map to pens. The mishap model is stylised: ordinary pens skip when the tip clogs or the paper is rough or very absorbent, and one forum report describes paper drifting during long plots, but none of this is calibrated to a specific machine. The page therefore labels the physics as an approximation and keeps the ideal SVG export honest. Perlin noise was formally described in a 1985 SIGGRAPH paper; sources disagree on whether it was first developed in 1982 or 1983, so the page leaves that date out.

sources.title: Flow Fields (Tyler Hobbs)
sources.snippet: Widely cited essay on flow fields; reported to note that Perlin noise is the usual way to initialise the vectors.
sources.note: Primary essay on the technique, seen as a search result only

sources.title: Getting Creative with Perlin Noise Fields (Sighack)
sources.snippet: Processing write-up explaining Perlin noise fields as a force field that steers particles, with source code and GIFs.
sources.note: Independent agreement that noise fields steer particle paths

sources.title: Noise in Creative Coding (Varun Ferreira)
sources.snippet: Tutorial covering the three steps of a noise-based vector field, particles dropped on it and traced paths, with damping.
sources.note: Third independent description of the flow-field mechanism

sources.title: Executing Generative Art with a Plotter (Tyler Hobbs)
sources.snippet: Essay on plotter work; reported to stress that a plotter only draws lines and cannot cover earlier ink, which constrains layering order.
sources.note: Single-source claim about plotter constraints; not independently confirmed

sources.title: vfab (PyPI)
sources.snippet: Plotter workflow tool that detects SVG layers and offers pen mapping for multi-layer designs.
sources.note: Layers map to pens in plotter workflows

sources.title: christmas2023 (GitHub project)
sources.snippet: An artist's pipeline generates SVGs, post-processes them with a plotter-vector tool and keeps layers separate for different pens.
sources.note: Independent confirmation of the layers-per-pen workflow

sources.title: How to stop a rollerball pen from skipping (Scriveiner)
sources.snippet: Explains skipping as caused by clogged tips from dried ink or paper fibres, and by paper surface affecting ink flow.
sources.note: Ordinary-pen physics for ink skipping; not plotter-specific

sources.title: Troubleshooting Fountain Pen Flow and Skipping (Ferris Wheel Press)
sources.snippet: Lists dried ink, debris and paper type among causes of skipping and poor flow.

sources.title: graphtec 8600 drawing pen with new paper type (Signs101 forum)
sources.snippet: Forum thread in which a long plot shifts sideways, attributed to paper sliding through the rollers.
sources.note: Single forum report of paper creep; unverified anecdote

sources.title: Perlin noise (Wikipedia)
sources.snippet: Encyclopedia article on the noise function Ken Perlin developed after working on a 1982 film, later described in a 1985 SIGGRAPH paper.
sources.note: Background and 1985 paper date; development year differs in other results

sources.title: Noise (The Book of Shaders)
sources.snippet: Shader tutorial noting that Perlin introduced gradient noise in 1985 to reduce the blocky look of value noise.

facts.claim: A flow field is a grid of direction vectors; particles dropped onto it and traced along it produce smooth curves, and Perlin noise is the common way to set the vector angles (as of 2026-10-10).
Plotter workflows keep artwork in separate SVG layers that are mapped to different pens.
Ordinary pens skip when the tip is clogged by dried ink or fibres and when the paper surface hampers ink flow; the page borrows this as a stylised model, not a plotter calibration.
Perlin's gradient noise was described in a 1985 SIGGRAPH paper.
Reported but unconfirmed: a plotter can only draw lines and cannot cover earlier ink, so layer order matters (per Tyler Hobbs's plotter essay, seen in a search result only).

design.coreLoop: Pick a composition and a seed, press plot, and watch the pen draw in real time while the operator log narrates events. The mishap dial changes how often ink skips, blots appear, the paper creeps or a pen swap lands slightly off. An ideal-versus-actual ghost toggle shows what the machine meant to draw, so each seed becomes a small experiment and the dial setting that flatters a given composition is the thing to find.
sophisticationHooks: Three seeded composition engines (flow-field ribbons with spacing control, L-system shrubs, spiral-packed circles) split across 2 to 3 pen layers

Stylised machine model: ink reservoir that depletes with distance and recovers on re-dip, touchdown blots, cumulative paper creep that misregisters later layers, with all randomness drawn from the seed so the URL reproduces the same plot
Operator log with deadpan one-line entries per event and an ideal-versus-actual ghost overlay
Exports: layered SVG of the ideal paths (labelled as ideal) and a PNG of the as-plotted poster with a plot-number caption
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: pure path generators and plotter-state model in a worker, canvas2d renderer with per-pen ink look, playback controls (speed, pause, skip to end), mishap dial plus 4 individual toggles, hash state (composition, seed, pens, dial), SVG and PNG export through Blob downloads, light/dark paper themes, reduced-motion path (instant draw), about/making-of panel. Cut: real G-code, stepper-motor audio, user-drawn input paths, more than 3 composition engines.
risks: The mishap physics is stylised and not calibrated to a real machine; the UI says so and the dossier keeps the plotter-constraint claim flagged as reported, unconfirmed.
Ordinary-pen skipping sources are not plotter-specific, so the about panel presents them as inspiration only.
Performance: long plots can reach tens of thousands of segments, so segments are batched, capped (about 60k) and drawn incrementally to a backing canvas.
Dial and toggle count could crowd a 360px layout; the controls fold into a drawer on small screens.
Flow-field ribbons are a very familiar look; differentiation relies on the machine-error layer and log, which needs strong writing and visible payoffs.
